title: Deadlocks increase sharply during peak traffic
description: Diagnose and eliminate deadlocks that appear only under concurrency, including lock ordering, snapshot isolation, and transaction-scoping fixes in SQL Server and EF Core.

data.text: Deadlocks are not random. They are deterministic consequences of concurrent transactions competing for the same resources in different orders. Under normal traffic, the timing never aligns. During peak traffic, the probability of circular wait rises sharply. SQL Server detects the cycle, chooses a victim, and aborts its transaction. If your application does not handle the 1205 error, the user sees a failure. If it does, the retry masks a deeper design problem.

data.title: Core concepts
items: Deadlock: two or more transactions hold locks that the other needs, causing indefinite wait
Lock escalation: the database converts fine-grained locks into coarse-grained ones under memory pressure
Isolation level: controls how transaction changes are visible to other transactions, affecting lock behavior
Snapshot isolation: reads versioned rows instead of locking, reducing read-write blocking
Access ordering: enforcing a deterministic resource acquisition order eliminates circular waits

terms.definition: A condition where two or more transactions hold locks that the other transactions need, causing all to wait indefinitely.
When a database engine converts many fine-grained locks into fewer coarse-grained locks to reduce memory overhead, increasing contention.
A database setting that controls how transaction changes are visible to other transactions, affecting locking behavior and deadlock probability.
The transaction SQL Server chooses to abort when a deadlock is detected, based on cost and deadlock priority.

items: Transactions access tables in inconsistent orders (e.g., T1 locks A then B, T2 locks B then A)
Long-running transactions hold locks across user think time or external API calls
High concurrency on hot tables with frequent updates and selects
Lock escalation from row locks to page or table locks under memory pressure
Missing or inefficient indexes causing table scans and wider lock footprints
READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT disabled, causing more blocking reads

cards.title: Access Ordering
cards.description: Ensure all transactions access resources in the same deterministic order (e.g., by primary key).
cons: Hard to enforce in existing large codebases
Does not help with lock escalation

cards.title: Snapshot Isolation
cards.description: Use READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT or SNAPSHOT to reduce blocking by reading versioned rows instead of locking.
cons: Not suitable for all consistency requirements

cards.title: Short Transactions
cards.description: Break large transactions into smaller units and commit early to reduce lock hold time.
cons: More round trips to the database

data.caption: Classic deadlock cycle between two transactions
data.definition:
graph LR
    T1[Transaction 1] -->|Holds| L1[Lock on Order]
    T1 -->|Needs| L2[Lock on Customer]
    T2[Transaction 2] -->|Holds| L2
    T2 -->|Needs| L1
    L1 -->|Blocked| T2
    L2 -->|Blocked| T1

items: Enable deadlock tracing in SQL Server Extended Events or the PostgreSQL log_lock_waits setting.
Analyze the deadlock graph to identify the objects, queries, and isolation levels involved.
Check whether both transactions modified the same tables in different orders.
Review recent schema or index changes that may have altered execution plans.
Test the fix in a load test that replicates peak concurrency before deploying.

data.title: Retry is a band-aid
data.text: Retrying deadlocked transactions reduces user-visible errors but does not fix the underlying race condition. Use retries as a safety net, not the primary solution.

items: Standardize table access order across all application services
Enable READ COMMITTED SNAPSHOT to reduce read-write blocking
Keep transactions short: do not include user think time or external API calls inside a transaction
Use the lowest practical isolation level: READ COMMITTED before REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE
Add covering indexes to eliminate key lookups that widen lock footprints
Monitor deadlock graphs continuously and alert on spikes above baseline

items.question: Should I set DEADLOCK_PRIORITY LOW globally?
items.answer: Setting DEADLOCK_PRIORITY LOW makes the current session the victim when a deadlock occurs. It reduces user-facing errors but does not prevent the deadlock. Use it alongside structural fixes.

items.question: Does snapshot isolation eliminate all deadlocks?
items.answer: No. Snapshot isolation reduces read blocking but update conflicts and write-write deadlocks can still occur. Use it to reduce frequency, not as a complete solution.

data.title: Analyze and fix a deadlock-prone query pattern
data.description: Given two stored procedures that update Orders and Customers in opposite orders, rewrite them to eliminate the deadlock risk and explain why the fix works.
steps: Read the deadlock graph from Extended Events
Identify the lock order conflict between the two procedures
Rewrite both procedures to access tables in the same order
Run a concurrency test with 100 parallel sessions to verify the deadlock no longer occurs
Document the change in a migration script
data.expectedOutcome: A deterministic lock order that prevents circular waits and a test proving deadlock frequency dropped to zero under peak concurrency.

data.title: Summary
points: Deadlocks are a concurrency problem, not a hardware problem
Access tables in a consistent order to eliminate circular waits
Snapshot isolation reduces blocking but does not remove all deadlocks
Keep transactions short and avoid user think time inside transactions
Monitor deadlock graphs and act on trends, not isolated incidents
data.takeaway: Deadlocks are predictable in concurrent systems. Design your data access patterns to remove the circular wait condition rather than relying on retries alone.
